**The register of designations allocated since August 1998, which Andreas Parsch compiles from data the Department of Defense has released, holds 539 rows in the copy he last updated on 23 August 2026, and its mission statements are built from three verbs.** Eighteen entries say demonstrate, five say investigate, and one says validate. Every one of those verbs takes a capability as its object. **Exactly one entry in the register uses the verb exhibit, and its object is a failure mode** \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum, MDS Designators Allocated After 19 August 1998][ref_mds_addendum]\].

This is the fifty-seventh article in the [X-Planes series][related_post_a297_framing], following the [X-1][related_post_a298_bell_x1], the [X-2][related_post_a299_bell_x2], the [X-54][related_post_a351_gulfstream_x54], and the [X-55][related_post_a352_lockheed_martin_x55].

**Every other aeroplane in this series was designed so that flutter would not happen, and was cleared against a boundary it was never meant to reach.** This one was designed so that flutter would happen, inside the envelope rather than beyond it, and it was eventually flown into that boundary on purpose with the suppression switched off to watch \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\].

**The word eventually is doing a great deal of work in that sentence, and the article ends by explaining it.** The flutter research is the part of this programme that nearly did not happen, and the cause had nothing to do with flutter \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\].

## The Research Question

**The question this aeroplane existed to settle is whether the flutter margin an aeroplane carries as structure could be supplied instead by a control system.** The article states that proposition in those terms where it discusses the regulatory margin below, and the programme's stated goal of increasing aspect ratio by thirty to forty percent is the commercial form of the same question \[[X-56A Multi-Utility Technology Testbed, NASA Facts FS 2015 08 105 AFRC][ref_x56_factsheet]\].

**The question can only be answered by an aeroplane that flutters inside its envelope**, because a control law that suppresses an instability cannot be validated against a vehicle that never becomes unstable. The register states the vehicle's purpose as the exhibition of multiple flutter mechanisms within its flight envelope \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum, MDS Designators Allocated After 19 August 1998][ref_mds_addendum]\]. The next three subsections set out that entry, the physics of the instability it names, and the margin the aeroplane was built without.

### The Registry Entry Is the Primary Document

**The register records the following against X-56A, allocated on 7 January 2012** to Lockheed Martin, powered by two Jetcat turbojets, and sponsored by the United States Air Force \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum, MDS Designators Allocated After 19 August 1998][ref_mds_addendum]\].

> A remotely piloted, high aspect ratio, flying wing vehicle designed to exhibit multiple flutter mechanisms within its flight envelope.

The register is a public addendum to DOD 4120.15-L, the Department of Defense's official list of aircraft and missile designations. Andreas Parsch compiles it from official Department of Defense sources obtained under the Freedom of Information Act and maintains it alongside the same site's allocation list \[[DOD 4120.15-L, Model Designation of Military Aerospace Vehicles][ref_dod_412015l]\] \[[Allocation of Official Aerospace Vehicle MDS Designations][ref_mds_allocation]\] \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum, MDS Designators Allocated After 19 August 1998][ref_mds_addendum]\]. **Its descriptions are not all official wording.** The compiler marks the descriptions he could not take from officially released data, and six of the eighteen that say demonstrate are among them, while the X-56A's, dated 2012, is official \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum, MDS Designators Allocated After 19 August 1998][ref_mds_addendum]\].

Of the 539 allocation rows the addendum carries, this is **the only one containing the word flutter, the only one containing any form of the word exhibit, the only one naming a flying wing, the only one naming a high aspect ratio, and the only one naming a flight envelope**. Those five measurements are separate, and each returns one row, the same row.

**The copy these counts come from is later than this article's date.** The version current on that date, the compiler's update of 11 August 2025 as the Internet Archive captured it on 25 November 2025, held 526 rows, twenty-nine of them X rows \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum, 11 August 2025][ref_mds_addendum_2025]\]. In it seventeen entries say demonstrate, five of them among the descriptions the compiler marks, because the X-76A row had not yet been entered. It gave eight rows a question mark in the date field and marked seventeen rows as not drawn from Department of Defense records, because it still carried a questioned date for a supersonic target converted from an anti-radiation missile, still listed the F-47 fighter, and did not yet list the long range air to air missile. **Every finding about the X-56A and the X-56B holds in both versions**, being the five terms found in that row alone, the single use of exhibit, the counts of the other two verbs and of the counterexample terms, the X-56B as the only X row with a questioned date, and the X-37B and the X-56B as the only marked X rows.

**The uniqueness that matters is not any single one of them.** It is the verb. A register of experimental aircraft is a register of intentions, and the intentions it records are overwhelmingly to demonstrate that something works. **To exhibit a flutter mechanism is to undertake that something will fail**, in a controlled way, at a place of one's choosing.

**The claim needs testing against its strongest counterexample.** The counterexample here is real. The X-54A was to be `capable of generating relevant ground sonic boom signatures`, and the X-59A `will create a shaped sonic boom signature` \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum, MDS Designators Allocated After 19 August 1998][ref_mds_addendum]\] \[[X-Planes: Gulfstream X-54][related_post_a351_gulfstream_x54]\]. **Both of those aeroplanes were also designed to produce an unwanted phenomenon on purpose.** Two entries mention a sonic boom, one mentions vortices, two mention icing, one mentions fatigue.

**The distinction that survives the counterexample is sharper than the one that did not.** A sonic boom is a nuisance on the ground and it does not threaten the aeroplane making it. Icing and fatigue are conditions an aeroplane is exposed to. **Flutter often ends in structural failure, and an aeroplane can pass from stable to unstable within a few knots of airspeed** \[[Kehoe, A Historical Overview of Flight Flutter Testing, NASA TM-4720][ref_kehoe_flight_flutter]\]. The X-56A is the only entry in the register whose stated purpose is to produce a phenomenon capable of destroying the vehicle produced to demonstrate it.

### The Physics of Flutter

**Flutter is not a vibration that gets worse.** It is a transfer of energy from the airstream into the structure, mediated by the phase between how a surface moves and how the air pushes back \[[Aeroelasticity][ref_aeroelasticity]\] \[[Bisplinghoff, Ashley and Halfman, Aeroelasticity][book_bisplinghoff]\].

**Flutter is the dynamic one of the two classical aeroelastic instabilities** \[[Flutter, Aeroelasticity][ref_flutter_wikipedia]\]. The other is divergence, which is static, and which occurs when the aerodynamic moment twisting a wing exceeds the structural moment resisting it, at which point the twist runs away without any oscillation at all \[[Aeroelasticity, Divergence][ref_divergence]\] \[[Dowell, A modern course in aeroelasticity][book_dowell]\].

Two structural modes are usually enough. Each has a frequency and a shape, and the pair defines a normal mode \[[Normal Mode][ref_normal_mode]\], and each is damped by some fraction of the damping that would suppress oscillation entirely \[[Damping Ratio][ref_damping_ratio]\]. **Measuring those frequencies and dampings on a real structure is a separate discipline** \[[Ewins, Modal testing, theory and practice][book_ewins]\], and the X-56 programme did it on the ground before it did it in the air. As airspeed rises the aerodynamic forces grow, the frequencies move, and at some speed two of them approach one another closely enough to couple. **Once they couple, the damping of one mode falls and the damping of the other rises**, and at the speed where the falling one reaches zero the structure will sustain an oscillation on the energy the airflow supplies. **Above that speed the damping is negative and the amplitude grows every cycle** \[[Wright and Cooper, Introduction to aircraft aeroelasticity and loads][book_wright_cooper]\] \[[Hodges and Pierce, Introduction to structural dynamics and aeroelasticity][book_hodges_pierce]\].

**What is measured is damping, taken from how an oscillation decays.** Strike a structure, watch consecutive peaks, and the ratio between them gives the logarithmic decrement \[[Damping Ratio][ref_damping_ratio]\] \[[Ewins, Modal testing, theory and practice][book_ewins]\].

$$
\Delta = \ln\!\left(\frac{x_n}{x_{n+1}}\right)= \frac{2\pi\zeta}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^{2}}}
$$

$$
\frac{x_{n+1}}{x_n} = \exp\!\left(\frac{-2\pi\zeta}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^{2}}}\right)
$$

**That relation is the reason the X-56A programme could set a numerical gate on proceeding.** Its requirement was a closed loop damping ratio above 0.04 at every cleared condition \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\].

$$
\zeta_c > 0.04
$$

$$
\zeta = 0.04 \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac{x_{n+1}}{x_n} = 0.778
$$

**The gate requires, in effect, that a disturbance lose about 22 percent of its amplitude every cycle** \[[Damping Ratio][ref_damping_ratio]\]. The margin is small, roughly that of a structure that rings four or five times after being struck. The aeroplane was required to hold it while flying above the speed at which the same structure, uncontrolled, would have had none at all.

**The consequence is that flutter has no useful warning margin in the ordinary sense.** A structure at ninety-five percent of its flutter speed is not slightly fluttering. It is stable, and it will look stable, and the quantity that is about to go through zero is a damping ratio that no one aboard can feel. **For this reason flutter is cleared by prediction and margin rather than by approaching it and observing**, and the X-56A was built to break that convention \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\].

The most widely known flutter event is not an aeroplane at all. The Tacoma Narrows bridge deck of 1940 is the canonical case, and bridge aerodynamics treats the flutter boundary as a routine design quantity \[[Tacoma Narrows Bridge, 1940][ref_tacoma_narrows]\] \[[Simiu and Scanlan, Wind effects on structures][book_simiu_scanlan]\]. **The comparison is central here**, because this article's reference survey is built on the observation that a bridge deck and a wing are the same problem with different boundary conditions.

### The Margin the Regulation Requires

**A transport aeroplane is required to be free from flutter at every speed up to a margin above its design dive speed.** The airworthiness requirement is fifteen percent in equivalent airspeed above the design dive speed, and the design dive speed already sits above the maximum operating speed \[[14 CFR 25.629, Aeroelastic Stability Requirements][ref_far_25_629]\] \[[14 CFR 25.335, Design Airspeeds][ref_far_25_335]\]. **In the X-56 programme's summary of this convention, aircraft typically carry around enough structure to keep flutter fifteen percent above the design dive speed** \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\].

$$
V_F \;\ge\; 1.15 \, V_D
$$

**The choice of equivalent airspeed for the requirement matters.** Flutter depends on dynamic pressure rather than on speed \[[Dynamic Pressure][ref_dynamic_pressure]\], and dynamic pressure is the quantity that equivalent airspeed is constructed to preserve \[[Equivalent Airspeed][ref_equivalent_airspeed]\].

$$
q = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho V^{2}
$$

$$
V_E = V \sqrt{\frac{\rho}{\rho_0}} = V \sqrt{\sigma}
$$

$$
\frac{q_F}{q_D} \;\ge\; 1.15^{2} = 1.3225
$$

**A fifteen percent speed margin is a thirty-two percent margin in the quantity that drives the instability** \[[14 CFR 25.629, Aeroelastic Stability Requirements][ref_far_25_629]\], because dynamic pressure goes as the square of speed. **The regulation is written in speed and paid for in pressure**, and the factor between the two makes the structural penalty as large as it is.

The flying was done from a lake bed about 2,300 feet above sea level \[[Rogers Dry Lake][ref_rogers_dry_lake]\], where the standard atmosphere gives a density ratio a little under unity \[[U.S. Standard Atmosphere][ref_us_standard_atmosphere]\] \[[True Airspeed][ref_true_airspeed]\].

$$
\sigma = \frac{1.145}{1.225} = 0.934, \qquad \sqrt{\sigma} = 0.967
$$

$$
q_1 = \tfrac{1}{2}(1.145)(57.1)^{2} = 1.87 \times 10^{3}
$$

**The first mechanism therefore arrives at about 1.87 kilopascals**, a little under two percent of an atmosphere pressing on the wing.

**Two aeroplanes at the same equivalent airspeed and different altitudes are at the same dynamic pressure and therefore at the same point relative to a flutter boundary**, while their true airspeeds differ by the square root of the density ratio \[[Equivalent Airspeed][ref_equivalent_airspeed]\] \[[True Airspeed][ref_true_airspeed]\] \[[U.S. Standard Atmosphere][ref_us_standard_atmosphere]\]. **Every speed quoted in this article is the speed its source quotes**, and the flight test report works in knots without stating a conversion, a defensible choice for an aeroplane whose envelope lies within a few thousand feet of a dry lake bed.

**The phrase carry around enough structure states the economic argument in four words.** Torsional and bending stiffness are bought with material, material is weight, and weight is fuel. **The flutter margin is therefore a mass penalty paid on every flight of every aeroplane in the fleet**, in exchange for the assurance that a boundary is never approached.

**The proposition the X-56 exists to test is that the margin could be supplied by a control system instead of by structure.** That proposition has a long history, and a published assessment of where it stands is the natural place for a reader to go next \[[Livne 2018][research_livne_2018]\]. If a feedback law can add damping to the mode that is losing it, the boundary moves, and the structure does not have to be as stiff. **The wing may then be longer and thinner, which reduces induced drag, and lighter, which reduces everything.** The programme's stated goal was to increase aspect ratio by thirty to forty percent \[[X-56A Multi-Utility Technology Testbed, NASA Facts FS 2015 08 105 AFRC][ref_x56_factsheet]\].

**The aeroplane therefore had to flutter.** Validating a suppression law requires a structure that goes unstable. **The demonstration requires the failure mode to be present, reachable, survivable and repeatable**, and no aeroplane certified under the ordinary rule offers any of those four.

## Programme Origin, The Wreck Behind the Programme

**A flying wing of very high aspect ratio had already been lost, and the X-56A modelling work cites its investigation as showing the importance of a time domain form of the models** \[[Ouellette 2017][research_ouellette_2017]\].

The Helios Prototype was a solar powered flying wing built to fly very high for a very long time, and the last of a line that had begun with Pathfinder \[[NASA Pathfinder][ref_pathfinder]\]. On 26 June 2003, flying from the Pacific Missile Range Facility on Kauai, it encountered turbulence of a kind the crew considered ordinary. **The disturbance produced an abnormally high wing dihedral**, the aircraft entered an undamped pitch oscillation, the airspeed excursions grew with every cycle until the design speed was exceeded, and the resulting dynamic pressure tore the leading edge secondary structure and the upper surface skin off the outer panels \[[NASA Releases Helios Prototype Aircraft Mishap Report][ref_helios_mishap]\] \[[NASA Helios Prototype][ref_helios_wikipedia]\] \[[Noll et al. 2007][research_noll_helios_mishap]\].

**The mishap board's finding bears directly on the X-56A.** The mishap resulted from the inability to predict, using available analysis methods, the aircraft's increased sensitivity to atmospheric disturbances following configuration changes made for the long duration demonstration \[[NASA Releases Helios Prototype Aircraft Mishap Report][ref_helios_mishap]\].

**The theoretical problem the mishap exposed had already been identified.** Very flexible aircraft of high aspect ratio do not obey the linear equations that serve conventional aeroplanes, because the deflections are large enough that the geometry changes as the wing bends \[[Patil et al. 1999b][research_patil_hodges_1999]\]. **A later programme built a vehicle specifically to test that class of model in flight** \[[Cesnik et al. 2012][research_cesnik_senatore_2012]\], and the idea that a composite wing's stiffness can be laid up to bend in a chosen direction is older still \[[Weisshaar et al. 1998][research_weisshaar_nam_1998]\].

**The finding concerns a model, not a wing.** The aeroplane behaved in a way the available methods could not anticipate, in a flight condition nobody thought was extreme. **A programme whose response to that finding is to build a model is a programme that has understood it**, and a model of a highly coupled flexible aeroplane cannot be validated against an aeroplane that does not exhibit the coupling. The X-56A is the answer to Helios, and the register's verb is the answer stated in one word.

## Sizing From First Principles

**The programme's stated goal was to increase aspect ratio by thirty to forty percent, and both halves of that trade can be computed** \[[X-56A Multi-Utility Technology Testbed, NASA Facts FS 2015 08 105 AFRC][ref_x56_factsheet]\].

The prize is induced drag. For a wing of given lift coefficient and span efficiency, induced drag falls as aspect ratio rises \[[Aspect Ratio, Aeronautics][ref_aspect_ratio]\] \[[Megson, Aircraft structures for engineering students][book_megson]\].

$$
C_{D_i} = \frac{C_L^{2}}{\pi \, AR \, e}
$$

$$
\frac{C_{D_i}(\Lambda \cdot AR)}{C_{D_i}(AR)} = \frac{1}{\Lambda}
$$

$$
\Lambda = 1.3 \Rightarrow 0.769, \qquad \Lambda = 1.4 \Rightarrow 0.714
$$

**Neither the lift coefficient nor the span efficiency survives into the ratio** \[[Aspect Ratio, Aeronautics][ref_aspect_ratio]\], so this part of the trade is parameter free. **Thirty percent more aspect ratio is 23.1 percent less induced drag and forty percent is 28.6 percent**, and no property of the particular aeroplane is needed to say so.

**The price is the flutter speed, and computing it requires knowing how the two coalescing frequencies move.**

Treat the wing as a uniform cantilever, which is an idealisation and is flagged as one. Its fundamental bending frequency is set by stiffness, mass per length and the fourth power of the semispan \[[Ewins, Modal testing, theory and practice][book_ewins]\] \[[Hodges and Pierce, Introduction to structural dynamics and aeroelasticity][book_hodges_pierce]\].

$$
\omega_b = \frac{(\kappa_1 L)^{2}}{L^{2}} \sqrt{\frac{EI}{m'}},\qquad \kappa_1 L = 1.8751
$$

$$
\omega_b \;\propto\; \frac{1}{L^{2}} \sqrt{\frac{EI}{m'}}
$$

**The bracketed group is the standard cantilever coefficient**, 1.8751 squared, or 3.516, which the boundary conditions fix independently of any particular wing.

**The short period frequency, by contrast, rises with airspeed**, because the aerodynamic restoring moment that sets it grows with dynamic pressure \[[Nelson, Flight stability and automatic control][book_nelson]\] \[[Stengel, Flight dynamics][book_stengel]\].

$$
\omega_{sp} \;\propto\; V
$$

**Body freedom flutter occurs where the rising one meets the nearly stationary one** \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\] \[[Aeroelasticity][ref_aeroelasticity]\].

$$
\omega_{sp}(V_F) \;=\; \omega_b
$$

$$
V_F \;\propto\; \omega_b \;\propto\; \frac{1}{L^{2}} \sqrt{\frac{EI}{m'}}
$$

**The flutter speed thus inherits the wing bending frequency's scaling exactly.** It rises with the square root of bending stiffness and falls with the square of the semispan \[[Bisplinghoff, Ashley and Halfman, Aeroelasticity][book_bisplinghoff]\] \[[Wright and Cooper, Introduction to aircraft aeroelasticity and loads][book_wright_cooper]\].

Now raise the aspect ratio. At fixed wing area the span goes as the square root of aspect ratio \[[Aspect Ratio, Aeronautics][ref_aspect_ratio]\] \[[Flying Wing][ref_flying_wing]\].

$$
b = \sqrt{AR \cdot S} \;\propto\; \sqrt{AR}
$$

$$
\frac{EI(\Lambda \cdot AR)}{EI(AR)}= \left(\sqrt{\Lambda}\right)^{4} = \Lambda^{2}
$$

$$
\Lambda = 1.3 \Rightarrow 1.69, \qquad \Lambda = 1.4 \Rightarrow 1.96
$$

**The two halves of the trade can now be set side by side, and they are not the same size** \[[X-56A Multi-Utility Technology Testbed, NASA Facts FS 2015 08 105 AFRC][ref_x56_factsheet]\].

$$
C_{D_i} \;\times\; \Lambda^{-1}, \qquad EI \;\times\; \Lambda^{+2}
$$

**A factor in aspect ratio buys its reciprocal in induced drag and costs its square in bending stiffness.** Thirty percent more aspect ratio is 23.1 percent less induced drag and 69 percent more bending stiffness. Forty percent is 28.6 percent less drag and 96 percent more stiffness. **The structural price is the square of the aerodynamic prize, paid in weight.**

**That single relation is the commercial argument for this aeroplane.** If the flutter margin has to come from stiffness, the wing that is thirty percent more slender needs to be most of twice as stiff, and the weight of that stiffness eats the drag saving that motivated the slenderness. **If instead the margin can come from a feedback law, the exponent on the right hand side goes away.**

**The idealisation should be stated plainly.** A real wing is not a uniform cantilever, its mass per length is not constant, the short period frequency does not rise exactly linearly, and body freedom flutter involves the coupled system rather than either frequency alone. **What survives all of that is the exponent**, because the fourth power in the cantilever relation comes from the length scale and not from the mass distribution, and the square in the aspect ratio relation comes from the definition of aspect ratio. **The numbers are approximate. The shape of the trade is not.**

## Dependent Systems

**The systems this aeroplane depended on were chosen to make its experiment measurable, and the article treats them in two parts.** The first of the two subsections that follow records the airframe, the modular wing sets sharing one outer mould line, the turbojets, the control surfaces and sensors, and the ballistic parachute. The second records the configuration that produces the instability and the 325 state model built to predict it \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\].

**The model is counted here as a dependent system because the article treats the flight dynamics and the structural dynamics of this aeroplane as one problem**, and the model is the means by which the programme carried that one problem into flight.

### What Was Built

**The vehicle's conceptual design was published before it was built**, and reading it alongside the flight results is the cleanest way to see which of the intentions survived \[[Beranek et al. 2010][research_beranek_nicolai_2010]\] \[[Ryan and Bosworth 2014][research_ryan_x56_active_control]\]. **An account of the history and issues of developing its integrated flight and aeroelastic control system, by authors of that conceptual design, was published in 2016** \[[Burnett et al. 2016][research_burnett_beranek_2016]\].

**Two nearly identical aircraft were designed and built at Palmdale by the Lockheed Martin Skunk Works for the Air Force Research Laboratory** \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\] \[[Skunk Works][ref_skunk_works]\] \[[Air Force Research Laboratory][ref_afrl]\].

The vehicle is small. It has a wingspan of 28 feet and a length of about 7.5 feet, and its maximum gross takeoff weight is given as 525 pounds in the flight test report and 550 pounds in the programme retrospective, against about 480 pounds in the fact sheet \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\] \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\] \[[X-56A Multi-Utility Technology Testbed, NASA Facts FS 2015 08 105 AFRC][ref_x56_factsheet]\]. **The article leaves the three weights from three documents of one programme unreconciled**, and uses the flight test report's figure throughout because that document reports the flight results those weights condition.

Propulsion is two Jetcat P400 turbojets of about 90 pounds of thrust each \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\] \[[JetCat, Model Turbojet Engines][ref_jetcat]\]. **The register records the engine as the P-240 and the flight test report records it as the P400** \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum, MDS Designators Allocated After 19 August 1998][ref_mds_addendum]\]. The register is a record of what was allocated in January 2012 and the report is a record of what flew, so the disagreement is unremarkable, but it is a disagreement and this article does not conceal it.

**The mode the aeroplane was built to measure is a low frequency one.** Analysis before flight placed the first flutter mode at about 2.6 hertz near 101 knots equivalent airspeed \[[Pak 2012][research_pakchangi_2012]\], and an account of the control design places the suppressed flutter mode near 3 hertz and the first four structural modes between 3.2 and 10 hertz \[[Ryan and Bosworth 2014][research_ryan_x56_active_control]\]. The programme documents cited here do not state why turbojets were chosen rather than propellers, and the directory entry attributes the choice to the low frequency noise of propellers, which could have interfered with the flutter tests \[[Lockheed Martin X-56 MUTT, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_x56_dsn]\].

**The other half of the programme's purpose is gusts, which this article treats only in passing.** A flexible wing is loaded by atmospheric turbulence as well as by manoeuvre, the discipline of predicting those loads is old and well developed \[[Hoblit, Gust loads on aircraft, concepts and applications][book_hoblit]\], and gust load alleviation was named alongside flutter suppression in NASA's statements of what the X-56 was for \[[X-56A Multi-Utility Technology Testbed, NASA Facts FS 2015 08 105 AFRC][ref_x56_factsheet]\] \[[X-56A Multi-Utility Technology Testbed, NASA][ref_nasa_x56]\].

**The design is built around modularity.** The system comprised two centre bodies, one set of stiff wings and three sets of flexible wings, along with a ground control station and a trailer \[[X-56A Multi-Utility Technology Testbed, NASA Facts FS 2015 08 105 AFRC][ref_x56_factsheet]\]. Every wing set shares the same outer mould line and differs only in structural properties \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\].

**The arrangement builds a controlled experiment into the hardware.** The stiff wings put flutter outside the achievable envelope and were used to collect rigid body aerodynamic and control data and to prove out the aircraft systems. The flexible wings put at least one flutter mode well inside it \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\]. **The aerodynamics is held constant and the structure is the variable**, the only arrangement that can attribute a change in behaviour to flexibility rather than to shape.

There are ten trailing edge control surfaces, two body flaps and four wing flaps on each side, along with a three axis gyro set, an inertial unit with satellite navigation, and ten vertical accelerometers distributed through the wings and centre body \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\]. One set of flexible wings additionally carried fibre optic strain sensing \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\].

**The aeroplane also carried a ballistic parachute, intended to recover the fuselage and most of the aircraft systems in the event of an in-flight wing failure** \[[X-56A Multi-Utility Technology Testbed, NASA Facts FS 2015 08 105 AFRC][ref_x56_factsheet]\] \[[Ballistic Recovery Systems][ref_brs]\]. **A recovery system sized for losing a wing is a design document.** It shows what the programme thought might happen.

### Body Freedom Flutter and the Missing Tail

**The instability this aeroplane was built to produce is body freedom flutter**, and understanding why the configuration was chosen is understanding the vehicle \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\].

**A conventional aeroplane has a tail, and the tail sets the frequency of its short period pitch mode.** The short period is a rigid body oscillation in angle of attack and pitch rate, and on a tailed aeroplane its frequency is high because the tail is a long way from the centre of gravity and generates a large restoring moment \[[Etkin and Reid, Dynamics of flight][book_etkin]\] \[[Phugoid][ref_phugoid]\] \[[Short Period, Longitudinal Modes][ref_short_period]\] \[[Nelson, Flight stability and automatic control][book_nelson]\] \[[Stengel, Flight dynamics][book_stengel]\]. **The first wing bending mode is an elastic oscillation and its frequency is set by the stiffness and mass distribution of the wing.** On a conventional aeroplane these two frequencies are far apart, and modes that are far apart in frequency do not exchange energy.

**A tailless flying wing has neither of those separations** \[[Flying Wing][ref_flying_wing]\]. Its pitch inertia is low because there is no tail mass at a long arm, and its aspect ratio is high because that is the point of it, so the first wing bending frequency is low.

$$
AR = \frac{b^{2}}{S}
$$

**Aspect ratio is the quantity the programme is trying to increase** \[[Aspect Ratio, Aeronautics][ref_aspect_ratio]\], and it enters the problem twice. It reduces induced drag, the reason anyone wants it. **It also lowers the bending frequency of the wing, down into the band where the rigid body modes live.** The benefit and the hazard are the same geometric change. **The rigid body mode and the elastic mode end up in the same frequency band**, and the flight test report states plainly that the low pitch inertia and high aspect ratio of flying wings tends to cause rigid body flight modes and flexible modes to occur within the same frequency bands and to interact \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\].

The coupling itself has a clean physical description. **As the centre body pitches up, the wings bend symmetrically upward**, and that bending is in a phase relationship with the pitching that allows energy to pass between them \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\]. As airspeed increases the short period frequency rises and the first symmetric wing bending frequency falls slightly. **By about 100 knots the two are close enough to couple** \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\]. One pole moves left and becomes more stable, the other moves right, and at the speed where the second one crosses the imaginary axis the aeroplane is fluttering. **The picture is a root locus in which the parameter being varied is not a control gain but the dynamic pressure** \[[Root Locus Analysis][ref_root_locus]\].

**In this sense the aeroplane is not merely flexible but a different kind of dynamic system.** The flight dynamics and the structural dynamics are not two problems that can be solved separately and checked against one another. **They are one problem**, and the model the programme built reflects that. The methods by which it was built are published separately \[[Ouellette 2017][research_ouellette_2017]\] \[[Ouellette and Valdez 2020][research_ouellette_linear_models]\]. It carries 325 states, made up of 12 rigid body states, displacement and velocity for each of the first 25 structural modes, 93 aerodynamic lag states, 30 actuator states, 6 engine states and 134 sensor states \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\] \[[State-Space Representation][ref_state_space]\].

$$
n_s = 12 + 2\times 25 + 93 + 30 + 6 + 134 = 325
$$

**The 93 aerodynamic lag states answer a physical need.** A wing oscillating in a stream does not feel the forces a steady analysis would predict, because the flow has memory of where the surface was. **How much memory matters is set by the reduced frequency**, which compares the time the air takes to cross the chord with the period of the oscillation \[[Bisplinghoff, Ashley and Halfman, Aeroelasticity][book_bisplinghoff]\] \[[Dowell, A modern course in aeroelasticity][book_dowell]\].

$$
k = \frac{\omega_b \, \bar{c}}{2V}
$$

**When that number is not small, a steady theory cannot predict an oscillation at all**, and the lag states are how a state space model carries the memory that Theodorsen's function carries in the frequency domain \[[General Theory of Aerodynamic Instability and the Mechanism of Flutter][research_theodorsen_naca496]\]. **That paper dates from 1935 and remains the reference**, a point of note in an article whose survey is nearly three quarters contemporary.

**Those parts sum to exactly 325**, and the check matters, because a decomposition that does not add up is a misread decomposition. **The largest single block comes from neither the structure nor the aerodynamics.** The 134 sensor states outnumber the rigid body, structural and actuator states combined.

## The Flight Test Record

**The record counts fifty-four flights over both vehicles and every wing configuration, thirty-one of them in the flexible wing campaign at Armstrong from 2017 to 2019** \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\] \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\]. **The record is arranged in this article by what each part of it shows rather than by date.**

The first four subsections below report the flutter campaign. In it the envelope was expanded from 60 to 120 knots against a flutter onset between 111 and 114 knots, and the controller was frozen in flight so that the instability could be observed \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\] \[[X-56A Multi-Utility Technology Testbed, NASA][ref_nasa_x56]\].

The fifth reports the loss of the first vehicle on 19 November 2015, which came before that campaign. The sixth reports the ground drop tests and the changes made before the first flexible wing flight at Armstrong on 31 August 2017. The last reports the second mechanism, which was predicted and never reached.

### Finding a Boundary You Intend to Cross

**The problem of approaching a flutter boundary is that the quantity you need is the one that has not happened yet.** Damping is estimated from how a structure responds to a disturbance, and the estimate is only meaningful at the speed where it was taken. **Extrapolating a trend in damping toward zero is the traditional practice, and an unreliable one**, because damping trends can be nonlinear and stability can change abruptly within a few knots \[[Kehoe, A Historical Overview of Flight Flutter Testing, NASA TM-4720][ref_kehoe_flight_flutter]\].

The method the programme used instead is due to Zimmerman and Weissenburger, published as a conference paper in 1963 and in the Journal of Aircraft the following year \[[Zimmerman and Weissenburger 1964][research_zimmerman_weissenburger_1964]\] \[[Weissenburger and Zimmerman 1963][research_weissenburger_zimmerman_1963]\]. **It forms a single stability parameter out of the frequencies and damping of the two modes involved in the mechanism**, fits a second order curve to that parameter against airspeed, and takes the crossing of the axis as the predicted flutter speed \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\].

$$
F = \left[\left(\frac{\omega_2^{2}-\omega_1^{2}}{2}\right)+\left(\frac{\beta_2^{2}-\beta_1^{2}}{2}\right)\right]^{2}+ 4\,\beta_1\beta_2\left[\left(\frac{\omega_2^{2}+\omega_1^{2}}{2}\right)+ 2\left(\frac{\beta_1^{2}+\beta_2^{2}}{2}\right)\right]- \left(\frac{\beta_2-\beta_1}{\beta_1+\beta_2}\right)\left[\left(\frac{\omega_2^{2}-\omega_1^{2}}{2}\right)+ 2\left(\frac{\beta_1^{2}+\beta_2^{2}}{2}\right)\right]
$$

$$
F(V) = a V^{2} + g V + c, \qquad F(V_F) = 0
$$

**The parameter is defined only below the boundary.** That property makes it both useful and awkward. It gives an estimate of a speed the aeroplane has not reached from data taken where the aeroplane is safe, and it stops being defined at exactly the moment the answer would be observable.

**Its accuracy improved as the boundary was approached, a reassurance that also explains why the buildup had to be incremental.** With data only from low speed, far from flutter, the prediction was significantly wrong because the extrapolation was long. **From ten knots away it was within one knot** \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\]. For a predicted flutter speed $\hat{V}_F$ set against the observed $V_F$ of 111 knots, the relative error is therefore bounded by

$$
\frac{|\hat{V}_F - V_F|}{V_F} \;\le\; \frac{1}{111} = 0.0090
$$

which is under one percent.

**The lower order equivalent system method the programme fitted to its flight data is an old technique with a known literature** \[[Mitchell and Hoh 1982][research_mitchell_hoh_low_order]\] \[[Mitchell and Hoh 1981][research_mitchell_hoh_conference]\], and the multisine excitation and frequency domain estimation used to feed it were developed and reported across a series of papers by the same two authors \[[Grauer and Boucher 2018b][research_grauer_boucher_2018]\] \[[Grauer and Boucher 2018a][research_grauer_boucher_2018_b]\] \[[Grauer and Boucher 2019][research_grauer_boucher_2019]\] \[[Grauer and Boucher 2020c][research_grauer_boucher_2020]\] \[[Grauer and Boucher 2020a][research_grauer_boucher_2020_b]\] \[[Grauer and Boucher 2020b][research_grauer_bare_airframe]\].

**Alongside the damping estimates the programme performed system identification, recovering a dynamic model from measured inputs and outputs at every cleared condition** \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\] \[[System Identification][ref_system_identification]\], and it did so in the air on a vehicle whose model was the thing in question. The structure underneath it is an ordinary aircraft structure in every respect except how much it bends \[[Megson, Aircraft structures for engineering students][book_megson]\].

The envelope was expanded in ten knot increments until the predicted boundary was within ten knots, and in five knot increments after that. At each new condition the aeroplane was excited with a short doublet, called a rap, applied to the outboard surfaces, of 0.25 seconds and one to one and a half degrees of amplitude \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\].

**The requirement to proceed was the closed loop damping gate already stated**, and separately a gain margin above 3 decibels and a phase margin above 30 degrees \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\] \[[Gain Margin][ref_gain_margin]\] \[[Phase Margin][ref_phase_margin]\].

### The Two Stability Problems Disagree About Which Fuel State Is Dangerous

**The fuel tank is in the tail, with a consequence that needs careful statement** \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\].

As fuel burns, the centre of gravity moves forward, and a forward centre of gravity is more statically stable in pitch. **The report therefore records the greatest instability condition as occurring at takeoff**, with static pitch stability increasing as fuel is consumed \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\].

**The flutter boundary runs the other way.** At the low fuel and forward centre of gravity condition, flutter onset was found at about 111 knots. At the high fuel and aft centre of gravity condition it was about 114 knots \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\]. Writing $V_F^{\mathrm{fwd}}$ and $V_F^{\mathrm{aft}}$ for the flutter speeds in those two conditions, the shift with fuel state is

$$
V_F^{\mathrm{aft}} - V_F^{\mathrm{fwd}} = 114 - 111 = 3
$$

knots, a positive shift, so the aft condition flutters later.

**The fuel state that is statically safer is aeroelastically more dangerous.** The aeroplane is most statically unstable when it is full and least statically unstable when it is nearly empty, and it flutters earliest when it is nearly empty. **Three knots is not a large number, but the sign is the finding**, and the sign is the opposite of what a single intuition about stability would produce.

**The case illustrates a general fact at the centre of the programme.** Static stability and aeroelastic stability are different properties of the same aeroplane, they depend on the mass distribution in different ways, and improving one can degrade the other. **An aeroplane with two stability problems that disagree has to be cleared against both**, and neither clearance is evidence about the other.

### Flying Past the Boundary and Freezing the Controller

**The programme flew the aeroplane above its open loop flutter speed under active control, the result the vehicle existed to produce** \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\].

The flight campaign at the Armstrong Flight Research Center ran to 31 flights and expanded the airspeed from 60 to 120 knots, against a flutter onset between 111 and 114 knots \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\] \[[Armstrong Flight Research Center][ref_armstrong]\]. The flying was done over Edwards Air Force Base and Rogers Dry Lake, which has been the ground under many of the aeroplanes in this series \[[X-56A Multi-Utility Technology Testbed, NASA Facts FS 2015 08 105 AFRC][ref_x56_factsheet]\] \[[Edwards Air Force Base][ref_edwards]\] \[[Rogers Dry Lake][ref_rogers_dry_lake]\]. The programme retrospective describes the achievement as flying up to about ten percent past the open loop flutter instability \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\].

**Then they turned the control system off in flight** \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\].

The procedure is given here in full, because no other aeroplane in this series has realised the register's verb so directly. **A rap was applied to the outboard surfaces to excite the flutter mode with a repeatable amplitude larger than background turbulence.** Immediately after the rap, every control surface command was frozen at its current value and held, so that the uncontrolled dynamics of the aeroplane could be observed. **The duration was configurable in flight and was built up from one period of the flutter mode to three or four oscillations**, so that the damping could be measured. Then the control system was re-engaged and damped the motion out \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\].

**Below the boundary this showed low but positive damping. At the boundary it showed neutral stability. Above the boundary the damping was negative and the oscillation grew.** About two knots past onset the instability grew strongly enough that by the third open loop oscillation the dynamics were approaching test limits, and the airspeed progression for these particular test points was stopped \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\].

**Two knots.** The margin between an aeroplane that can be left uncontrolled for three cycles and one that cannot is two knots out of 111.

**How unstable is that, in the unit the gate was written in?** The test limit is not published \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\], so the question is answered as a bound rather than a measurement, by asking what negative damping would produce a given growth over three cycles \[[Damping Ratio][ref_damping_ratio]\].

$$
\zeta = -\frac{u}{\sqrt{1+u^{2}}}, \qquad u = \frac{\ln G^{1/3}}{2\pi}
$$

$$
G = 3 \Rightarrow \zeta = -0.058, \qquad G = 10 \Rightarrow \zeta = -0.121
$$

**A threefold growth over three oscillations implies a damping ratio of about minus 0.058, and a tenfold growth about minus 0.121** \[[Wright and Cooper, Introduction to aircraft aeroelasticity and loads][book_wright_cooper]\]. Both are the same order as the positive 0.04 the closed loop was required to hold. **The aeroplane was not far past its boundary in any absolute sense**, and the control system was not fighting an enormous instability. It was supplying a few percent of damping where the airflow was removing a few percent.

**That also explains why the open loop window was configured in cycles rather than in seconds** \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\].

$$
n_2 = \frac{\ln 2 \, \sqrt{1-\zeta^{2}}}{2\pi\,|\zeta|}
$$

$$
\zeta = -0.02 \Rightarrow n_2 = 5.5, \qquad \zeta = -0.05 \Rightarrow n_2 = 2.2
$$

**At a few percent of negative damping an oscillation doubles in a handful of cycles** \[[Normal Mode][ref_normal_mode]\], and the number of cycles depends only on the damping ratio while the number of seconds depends on the frequency as well. **A window measured in cycles means the same thing at every condition. A window measured in seconds does not.**

### The Limit Cycle the Suppressor Could Not See

**One of the most distinctive signs of being near the boundary was a small limit cycle oscillation in pitch, and its cause must be kept apart from the flutter.**

The limit cycle was produced by deadbands in the actuators \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\] \[[Deadband][ref_deadband]\] \[[Limit Cycle][ref_limit_cycle]\]. **The programme published a paper on this mechanism**, and its title, that deadbands tell no tails, states a finding \[[Pankonien et al. 2020][research_pankonien_deadbands]\]. An actuator with a deadband does not respond to a command below some threshold. **While the motion was inside that threshold the aeroplane was effectively open loop, and therefore unstable**, so the amplitude grew. Once the amplitude was large enough to push the actuators out of the deadband, the control system regained effectiveness and arrested the growth.

**The mechanism has a standard description, given here**, because it explains why the oscillation stopped growing as well as why it started. An actuator deadband is a nonlinearity, and its effect on a loop is captured by a describing function, which gives the effective gain it presents to a sinusoid of a given amplitude \[[Deadband][ref_deadband]\].

$$
N(A) = 1 - \frac{2}{\pi}\left[\arcsin\!\frac{d}{A}+ \frac{d}{A}\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{d}{A}\right)^{2}}\,\right],\quad A > d
$$

$$
\lim_{A \to d^{+}} N(A) = 0, \qquad \lim_{A \to \infty} N(A) = 1
$$

**The effective gain rises monotonically with amplitude.** A small oscillation sees almost no actuator authority, so the loop behaves as though it were open and the amplitude grows. As it grows the actuators spend more of each cycle outside the deadband, the effective gain rises, and the oscillation settles at the amplitude where the gain is just enough to restore marginal stability.

**The result is an aeroplane that is unstable in the small and stable in the large.** That inverts the usual arrangement, and it follows from the suppressor being unable to see what it was supposed to suppress. **The instability was bounded by the nonlinearity that caused it.**

### The Aeroplane Built to Flutter Was Destroyed by Rotation

**The first X-56A was lost on 19 November 2015 on its first takeoff with flexible wings, and it was not lost to flutter** \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\] \[[Lockheed Martin X-56 MUTT, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_x56_dsn]\].

The aircraft, operated by Lockheed Martin, had already flown a successful campaign with the stiff wings \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\]. **Immediately after rotation it pitched up, stalled, and crashed back onto the ground, a complete loss of the vehicle** \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\].

**The sources disagree on how many flights that campaign comprised, and the disagreement can be resolved.** The reference literature credits the aeroplane with sixteen flights before the accident \[[Lockheed Martin X-56 MUTT, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_x56_dsn]\] \[[Lockheed Martin X-56][ref_x56_wikipedia]\]. **The programme's retrospective, by contrast, records that Lockheed Martin flew eight flights with the stiff wings on the first centre body and that the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, NASA, flew eight with the stiff wings on the second** \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\]. **Sixteen is the total across both aircraft, and the aeroplane that was lost had made eight.** This article uses eight, because a count taken from the programme is better evidence than a count taken from reporting about it.

The mechanism has two parts and both are consequences of the design rather than accidents.

**The first is that the aeroplane is statically unstable.** On a statically stable aeroplane the aerodynamic centre is aft of the centre of gravity, so during rotation the lift force arrives nearly collocated with the main gear and produces little moment change. **On a statically unstable aeroplane the lift arrives well forward of the main gear**, and the result is a positive pitch acceleration exactly when the pilot is already commanding a pitch up \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\].

**The second is the flexibility itself.** During rotation the flexible wings bend upward as lift builds. That bending gives the wingtip a vertical velocity, vertical motion into the oncoming airflow reduces the local angle of attack, and reduced angle of attack reduces the tip lift. **On an aft swept wing, losing lift at the tip is a pitch up moment.** The programme estimated from wing video that this additional moment was likely enough to push the vehicle into stall \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\].

**The angle involved repays computation, because it is smaller than intuition suggests and still large enough to matter** \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\]. A section moving upward at some rate into a stream meets that stream at a reduced angle \[[Etkin and Reid, Dynamics of flight][book_etkin]\].

$$
\Delta\alpha = -\arctan\!\left(\frac{\dot{h}}{V}\right)
$$

$$
\dot{h} = 1,\; V = 65 \times 0.5144 = 33.4 \;\Longrightarrow\; \Delta\alpha = -1.71^{\circ}
$$

**At a takeoff speed of 65 knots, a wingtip rising at one metre per second loses 1.71 degrees of local angle of attack**, where the takeoff speed is the flight test report's and 0.5144 converts knots to metres per second \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\]. For comparison, the deliberate excitation used to provoke the flutter mode at the boundary was a control surface deflection of one to one and a half degrees. **A single metre per second of tip motion during rotation is the same order of disturbance as the input the programme used, years later, to make the aeroplane flutter on command.**

With $V_{TO}$ for that takeoff speed and $V_1$ for the lower flutter onset speed of 111 knots, the flutter boundary lay

$$
V_1 - V_{TO} = 111 - 65 = 46
$$

knots above it. **The aeroplane commissioned to exhibit an aeroelastic instability was destroyed by an aeroelastic effect near its takeoff speed of 65 knots, with the flutter boundary 46 knots away and entirely irrelevant.** The effect that killed it was a quasi-static coupling between wing bending and pitching moment, operating during the few seconds of rotation, in a regime the modelling effort had not been aimed at.

**The programme's explanation is unusually direct.** At the time of the mishaps, a piloted simulation with fully coupled structural dynamics was an active area of research for the team but was not a requirement for airworthiness. The fully coupled models that existed were built for the up and away condition and were not useful for a vehicle transitioning to or from the ground, and did not include landing gear dynamics \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\].

**The model was excellent where the research was and absent where the flying was.**

### Landing Was the Other Dangerous Part

**The same coupling threatened the other end of the flight, and this time it was caught before it cost an aeroplane.**

Ground drop tests conducted before the NASA flexible wing flights showed a significant reduction in nose bounce damping compared with the stiff wing and centre body only drops. **A large amount of energy went into the wings rather than the landing gear, the wing structure is very poorly damped compared with the gear, and wing bending couples into pitch** \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\]. The estimate was that the reduction in damping from stiff to flexible wings would likely produce an instability on landing.

The fixes were partly geometric and partly control. **The gear geometry was adjusted so the aeroplane sat at a higher angle of attack on the ground**, so that some lift was already present and less rotation was required, on the same principle that gives a B-52 its ground attitude. The main gear was moved forward, taking the tip back angle from about eighteen degrees to about ten. **And a controller was designed to actively damp the structural dynamics during landing** \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\].

**The first flexible wing flight at Armstrong was on 31 August 2017, and the actual takeoff and landing dynamics matched the fully coupled nonlinear simulation very well** \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\].

**The programme's summary of the risk allocation should be quoted whenever a testbed is designed.** Takeoff and landing were more risky than flutter testing, in part because the landing gear design was constrained by the parachute landing case rather than being optimised for normal landings \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\]. **You want your risk in the research under test, not in the normal operations of the testbed.**

### The Plural the Programme Did Not Deliver

**The register's noun is plural, and the plural is the one claim in the entry that the flight programme did not deliver.**

The first mechanism, body freedom flutter, was found between 111 and 114 knots depending on fuel state. **A second mechanism was predicted from the flight data, involving the first symmetric wing bending mode and the first symmetric wing torsion mode**, at 138 knots at low fuel and 144 knots at high fuel \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\].

**The maximum level flight speed of the aeroplane is 135 knots.** It can reach 150 knots in a dive \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\]. **The envelope was expanded to 120 knots** \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\]. With $V_2$ for the second mechanism's speed, $V_{\max}$ for the maximum level flight speed and $V_c$ for the highest airspeed cleared in flight, the gaps are

$$
V_2 - V_{\max} = 138 - 135 = 3 \;\text{to}\; 144 - 135 = 9, \qquad V_2 - V_c = 138 - 120 = 18
$$

knots. **The second mechanism sits between three and nine knots above anything the aeroplane can do in level flight**, and is reachable only in a descent. **The envelope stopped eighteen knots short of the second mechanism at its most optimistic.** The aeroplane never exhibited it.

$$
\frac{V_2}{V_1} = \frac{138}{111} = 1.243, \qquad \frac{q_2}{q_1} = \left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)^{2}= \left(\frac{138}{111}\right)^{2} = 1.55
$$

**The gap is larger than it looks, because flutter is a dynamic pressure before it is a speed.** With $V_1$ and $q_1$ for the first mechanism's speed and dynamic pressure and $q_2$ for the second's, reaching 138 knots from 111 requires 55 percent more dynamic pressure, not the 24 percent more airspeed that the two numbers suggest \[[Dynamic Pressure][ref_dynamic_pressure]\].

**Why the second mechanism was not reached is on record, and the cause was not aerodynamic.** The programme's retrospective states that the vehicle was capable of likely flying deeper into flutter and possibly getting close to the second flutter mode, and that with only one vehicle left the team became too risk averse, and that the Air Force Research Laboratory kept the project going just enough to get past flutter \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\].

**The register's plural was defeated by arithmetic about spare airframes.** The retrospective recommends building multiple vehicles at the beginning and planning to lose one or two, on the grounds that at this scale the vehicles cost little against engineering labour over the life of the programme, and that a single remaining vehicle forces a risk posture that prevents the research it was built for. **Three vehicles, it concludes, would likely have been the sweet spot** \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\].

**The finding is precise and unusual.** The entry in the register was not aspirational in the way an unbuilt aeroplane's entry is aspirational. The aeroplane was built, it flew, it fluttered, it was flown past its boundary under control, and the suppression was demonstrated by switching it off and on again \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\]. **Every clause of the mission statement was delivered except the plural**, and the plural failed for want of a spare airframe rather than for want of a mechanism.

## The Second Entry and Its Question Mark

**There are two X-56 rows and the second one is strange.**

The X-56B is recorded against Lockheed Martin with NASA as sponsor and a description of seven words, derivative of X-56A with a new wing. **Its date is given as 2019 followed by a question mark, and the question mark is the register's own** \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum, MDS Designators Allocated After 19 August 1998][ref_mds_addendum]\].

**The question mark bears measuring, because this register is otherwise precise to the day.** Of the 539 allocation rows, seven carry a question mark in the date field \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum, MDS Designators Allocated After 19 August 1998][ref_mds_addendum]\]. **The X-56B is the only X designation among them.**

The register also marks certain rows as not drawn from Department of Defense records. **Sixteen rows in the whole register carry that mark, and of the thirty-one X designation rows two carry it, the X-37B orbital test vehicle and the X-56B** \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum, MDS Designators Allocated After 19 August 1998][ref_mds_addendum]\]. The company they keep in that set is instructive. It consists of Stinger and Javelin variants, two training and test versions of a naval missile, a long range air to air missile, two Coast Guard helicopter variants, two prototypes for the collaborative combat aircraft, the Blackjack unmanned aircraft, and the RQ-170 Sentinel. **The X-56B's seven word description is consequently not official Department of Defense wording either.**

**The common property of that list is that the designation is known but the allocation record is not.** The list's legend describes these entries as designations that reliable sources confirm as official but that are missing, for reasons it calls unknown, from the officially released data \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum, MDS Designators Allocated After 19 August 1998][ref_mds_addendum]\].

**For the X-56B the reason appears to be that the vehicle was reconfigured rather than allocated.** The second airframe was reactivated in an improved configuration and flew again, and secondary sources place that first flight on 19 April 2021 and a crash shortly after takeoff on 9 July 2021 \[[Lockheed Martin X-56 MUTT, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_x56_dsn]\] \[[Lockheed Martin X-56][ref_x56_wikipedia]\]. **Those dates are two years after the date the register records with a question mark**, and this article does not resolve the discrepancy. It records that the register declines to assert the date, and that it does so for no other X designation.

**A register that marks its own uncertainty is a better document than one that does not.** Far from being a defect in the source, the question mark tells a reader which of its cells to trust less.

## Comparison With Ground Prediction

**The article reports four comparisons between what was predicted before a test point and what flight returned, and one prediction that flight never reached.** The predictions came from analysis, simulation, ground test and extrapolation in flight, and the article reports no wind tunnel prediction. Each comparison is argued in another section, and this one gathers them.

**The flutter boundary was predicted in flight from subcritical data rather than on the ground.** The method of Zimmerman and Weissenburger extrapolates a stability parameter toward zero from conditions where the aeroplane is safe. The prediction made from low speed data was significantly wrong, while one made ten knots short of the boundary fell within a knot of the observed 111 knots \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\]. The method and the figures appear under Finding a Boundary You Intend to Cross.

**The fully coupled models were built for the up and away condition and did not predict takeoff.** They were not useful for a vehicle transitioning to or from the ground and did not include landing gear dynamics, and the first vehicle was lost on rotation to a coupling between wing bending and pitching moment that the models had not been aimed at \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\]. The account of the loss on rotation above sets out the mechanism.

**Ground drop tests predicted a landing instability, and flight confirmed the simulation built in response.** The drops showed a significant reduction in nose bounce damping with the flexible wings, the gear geometry and a landing controller were changed, and on the first flexible wing flight at Armstrong the takeoff and landing dynamics matched the fully coupled nonlinear simulation very well \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\]. The landing subsection above reports it.

**The linear models used to design the control laws did not match flight in many areas.** The retrospective records that the control laws had to be retuned several times, that entire control surfaces were omitted from them because of poor matching, and that some of the differences are still not understood \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\]. The section headed What the Aeroplane Cost and What It Bought quotes that admission and argues its value.

**The second flutter mechanism was predicted from the flight data and never flown, so flight returned nothing to compare with it.** The prediction placed it at 138 knots at low fuel and 144 knots at high fuel, and the envelope stopped at 120 knots \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\].

**The record is silent on a comparison with the published conceptual design.** The design was published before the vehicle was built \[[Beranek et al. 2010][research_beranek_nicolai_2010]\], and the article recommends reading it alongside the flight results, but it does not set that design's predicted figures beside them. It reports no wind tunnel test of this configuration. A tunnel test of body freedom flutter needs a model free to pitch, and such tests have been made on a cable-mounted forward swept wing model \[[Chipman et al. 1985][research_chipmanr_rauchf_1985]\] and on a full-span flying wing in a suspension that releases pitch, plunge and yaw \[[Shi et al. 2020][research_shi_liu_2020]\].

## What the Aeroplane Cost and What It Bought

**Fifty-four flights were flown across the two vehicles and all wing configurations** \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\]. Thirty-one of those were the flexible wing campaign at Armstrong between 2017 and 2019 \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\]. **One vehicle was destroyed on the first flexible wing takeoff in 2015 and the surviving vehicle was lost in 2021 in its X-56B configuration** \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\] \[[Lockheed Martin X-56][ref_x56_wikipedia]\].

**What the programme bought is a set of flight measurements of a coupled flexible aeroplane past its own stability boundary**, made in free flight with the suppression switched off and on, which a tunnel model held in a suspension does not reproduce.

**What it also bought is a well documented disagreement between models and flight.** The retrospective records that many areas were found where the high fidelity up and away linear models did not match flight data, that control laws had to be retuned several times, that entire control surfaces were omitted from the laws because of poor matching, and that some of the differences are still not understood \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\].

**That last admission is the most valuable sentence in the programme's output.** A flight programme that reports agreement teaches nothing that the model did not already contain. **A flight programme that reports a disagreement it cannot yet explain, and keeps the data, has produced the only thing a testbed can produce that an analysis cannot.**

## What the Data Changed

**The flight data settled the central question in the affirmative, at one point in one aeroplane's envelope.** The X-56A was flown above its open loop flutter speed under active control, about ten percent past the open loop instability by the programme's account, against a requirement that the closed loop damping ratio stay above 0.04 at every cleared condition \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\] \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\]. **Freezing the controller in flight turned the flutter boundary from a prediction into a measurement**, with low but positive damping below it, neutral stability at it and a growing oscillation above it \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\].

**The data also showed how far a subcritical prediction of the boundary can be trusted.** The method of Zimmerman and Weissenburger was significantly wrong when fitted to low speed data and within one knot when fitted from ten knots away. That difference is the case for approaching a flutter boundary in shrinking increments rather than extrapolating to it from far below \[[Schaefer and others, Flying Beyond Flutter with the X-56A Aircraft, NASA TM 20220012337][ref_beyond_flutter]\].

**What the data did not settle is equally clear.** The second flutter mechanism, predicted at 138 to 144 knots across the two fuel states, was never flown, and the retrospective records that the linear models used to design the control laws did not match flight in many areas and that some of the differences are still not understood \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\]. The second airframe was reactivated in an improved configuration and flew again, and secondary sources date that first flight to 19 April 2021 \[[Lockheed Martin X-56 MUTT, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_x56_dsn]\] \[[Lockheed Martin X-56][ref_x56_wikipedia]\].

**The programme's most transferable finding concerns the testbed rather than the instability.** The ordinary phases of flight, takeoff and landing, carried more risk than the flutter testing did, and a single remaining vehicle forced a risk posture that prevented the research it was built for \[[Miller, X-56 Flight Test and Lessons Learned, Aerospace Control and Guidance Systems Committee Meeting 127][ref_x56_lessons]\].

### Body freedom flutter, which is the mechanism the configuration was chosen to produce

**The mechanism itself, in which the rigid body pitching of a tailless or flexible aircraft couples with the bending of its wing.** The records are analyses, wind tunnel tests and flight tests, mostly of flying wings and forward swept wings, and the coupled models of flight dynamics and aeroelasticity in which the coupling arises.

**40 of these 59 titles name body freedom flutter outright**, and the rest model the coupled flight dynamics and aeroelasticity in which it arises.
